newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Boeing /McDonnell probe in new phase.
newsitem.headline: EU Boeing /McDonnell probe in new phase.

text.p: The European Union's probe into a merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas has broken controversial new ground in focusing on Boeing moves to tie up airlines in long-term supply contracts.
The shift in the investigation comes as a surprise given that the EU's merger rules are not usually used to review commercial agreements.

But Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert made clear during a trip last week to the United States that he would not let pass such a golden opportunity to question Boeing's dominance of the world aviation market.

At issue was the conclusion last month of an exclusive pact between Boeing and Delta Air Lines Inc under which the airline committed itself to ordering all its new aircraft from the U.S. manufacturer in the next 20 to 25 years.
The deal was preceded by a similar agreement between Boeing and AMR's American Airlines. Continental Airlines is rumoured to be the next to sign up.

Although the Commission did not mention exclusive supply deals as one of its concerns when it opened a full investigation last month into the McDonnell merger, it became obvious last week that the probe would be used as a vehicle to tackle the issue.
Van Miert also left little doubt that he would accept nothing less than considerably shorter contracts.

"(The exclusive agreements) would lead to a situation where a big part of the market was closed, not just for a few years but for 15 or 20. This kind of practice cannot be accepted at all," Van Miert told a business audience on Wednesday in Atlanta.

The Commission can legally impose conditions for its clearance of the merger between Boeing and McDonnell if it concludes that the deal would harm fair competition in Europe, and exclusive contracts could be a target.

But that would be a rather unprecedented step, as the Commission's task under the merger rules is to prevent creation or strengthening of dominant positions. It does not usually accept "behaviourial commitments", such as that Boeing would no longer enter into long-terms exclusive deals, because this requires follow-up monitoring, antitrust lawyers stressed.
However, they predicted the EU would not miss the opportunity to interfere with the supply contracts.
"It's a bit of a gift for the Commission that Boeing needs clearance for its merger with McDonnell," one lawyer said.
In private, EU officials admit that their case would be stronger if competitors were to complain about the practice.
"If on top of that, we would receive complaints, we would also have to analyse (the contracts) under other articles of the (EU) treaty," a source close to Van Miert said on Friday.

The source was alluding to articles 85 and 86 which ban agreements or restrictive practices and abuse of a dominant position. The Commission can impose fines on companies which enter into such agreements if they refuse to change them.
Airbus Industrie, the only big competitor left in the commercial aircraft sector after the merger with McDonnell, is far from happy to have large clients cut off and has commented to the Commission.
"We don't think such monopolistic deals are in the best long-term interest of customers," an Airbus spokesman told Reuters.
He said Airbus has entered into long-term supply deals but without imposing an exclusivity clause. However, it fought neck-and-neck with Boeing for the Delta deal.
Airbus is a European consortium between Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas.
The Commission is not expected to rule on the Boeing/McDonnel merger before the end of July.

European airlines do not object to exclusive supply agreements, which they see as normal commercial decisions dictated mainly by price considerations, a spokesman at the Association of European Airlines told Reuters. - BRUSSELS NEWSROOM +32 2 287-6830
